are, essentially, inverses of each other. Many algorithms explicitly
treat them as inverse problems, where solving the problem in one
direction can inform the solution in the other direction.

In @sec-neural_nets, we described neural nets as being a
sequence of mappings from raw data to ever more abstracted
representations, layer by layer. This perspective puts representation
learning in the spotlight: deep learning is just representation
learning! Let us now point out an alternative perspective: in backward
order, deep nets are mappings from abstracted representations to ever
more concrete representations of the data, layer by layer. This backward
ordering is the direction in which deep generative networks work. This
perspective puts the spotlight on generative modeling: deep learning is
just generative modeling! Indeed both modeling directions are valid, and
the full picture looks like this
(@fig-generative_modeling_and_representation_learning-rep_gen_schematic):

![The relationship between representation learning and generative modeling. Here we label one side as "Data" and the other as "Embedding"; but what's the precise difference between these two things? Why is an RGB image data while a 100-dimensional vector of neural activations is an embedding? This is a question for you to think about; there is no correct answer.](./figures/generative_modeling_and_representation_learning/rep_gen_schematic.png){width="35%" #fig-generative_modeling_and_representation_learning-rep_gen_schematic}

:::{.column-margin}
Moving backward through a net is also what backpropagation does, but it computes a different function: backpropagation computes the gradient $\nabla f$ whereas here we focus on the inverse $f^{-1}$.
:::

black and white photo, it is a mapping

elements: Tall vertical bounding prism/cuboid with a wireframe outline showing the representation space

interactions.label: Process direction
interactions.teaches: Switches the active direction of information flow: bottom-up (encoding raw data into low-dimensional embeddings) vs. top-down (decoding abstract latents to generate concrete data samples)

interactions.label: Inspect Layer
interactions.teaches: Highlights a specific intermediate layer, visualizing how data representation complexity changes step-by-step

demo_steps.title: Hierarchical representations
demo_steps.narration: Observe the stacked layers. The lowest layer represents raw, high-dimensional 'Data' (like pixels), while the top layer represents highly abstracted 'Embeddings'. Each intermediate plane is a hidden layer that structures features at different levels of abstraction.

demo_steps.title: Representation learning (encoding)
demo_steps.narration: Watch the signals flow upwards. In representation learning, the network acts as an encoder: it maps complex, high-dimensional raw inputs into compressed, structured embeddings. As the points climb, local geometric details are discarded in favor of global semantics.

demo_steps.title: Generative modeling (decoding)
demo_steps.narration: Now look at the inverse direction: generating data from embeddings. By flowing downwards, a generative model decodes a compact latent point in the embedding space back into highly structured, concrete data coordinates on the bottom plane.

demo_steps.title: Layer-by-layer manifolds
demo_steps.narration: Select intermediate layers using the slider. Notice how the trajectories diverge and converge. Intermediate layers form transitional manifolds where representations are linearly untangled, making downstream classification or generation possible.

interactionPlan.camera_suggestion: An orthographic, slightly elevated three-quarter view looking down at the front corner of the vertical cuboid, showing both the top/bottom faces and the stacked vertical hierarchy clearly.
interactionPlan.view_reasoning: (1) The dominant vertical edges of the bounding prism run straight up and down on the page. (2) The base and top faces are drawn as diamonds with left and right edges receding symmetrically at roughly 30 degrees into the page. This indicates a camera positioned directly broadside to the front corner, implying an azimuth angle of exactly 45 degrees. (3) The top diamond's vertical squashing suggests a standard isometric tilt, placing the elevation angle around 30 to 35 degrees above the horizontal plane.

camera_view.view_notes: Orthographic projection is essential to maintain the clean isometric blueprint aesthetic of the original textbook illustration.

inline_constraints.default_view: Must match the original vertical orientation, containing the tall box with Data at the bottom and Embedding at the top, bordered by the dual vertical arrows.
inline_constraints.visible_ui: A single compact toggle for direction and one slider for layer inspection, placed neatly in the margins so they do not overlap the central prism.
inline_constraints.explainers: Use hover tooltips over the individual layers to show their relative level of abstraction (e.g., 'Layer 1: Low-level features' to 'Layer 3: Semantic parts').
inline_constraints.framing: Maintain a tall aspect ratio to match the vertical silhouette of the original figure.

interactionPlan.notes: Use simple THREE.CatmullRomCurve3 for the 3D spline pathways. Render glowing animated point particles (using canvas-mapped textures or simple round point materials) that trace these splines over time. The direction of particle travel should instantly reverse when the flow direction toggle is flipped.
